title: Rent Sets the Price: Why Rental Income Decides What a Commercial Property Is Worth
excerpt: Understand how net rental income, cap rates, lease terms and incentives shape a commercial property income scenario, then test your own assumptions.
author: Your Office Space
body:
Buy a house and the price comes down to the kitchen, the street and what sold next door.

Buy a commercial property and there's a much bigger question:

**How much rent does it earn, and how secure is it?**

In commercial property, the income is the asset. Two identical buildings on the same street can be worth very different amounts, simply because of the lease inside them.

Whether you're buying your own premises, investing through your [SMSF](/buyers-agency) or signing a lease, understanding this gives you an edge. Here's how it works, in plain English.

> **Want to see the numbers for your property or lease?** Our free [Commercial Rent Calculator](/resources/commercial-rent-calculator) shows the full cost of a lease over its term, and what that rent means for value.

---

## The simple formula behind most commercial values

Most commercial property is valued, at least in part, by its income. The basic maths looks like this:

**Value = Net income ÷ Cap rate**

- **Net income** (often called net operating income, or NOI) is the rent the owner receives in a year, less the costs the owner pays and can't recover from the tenant.
- **Cap rate** (capitalisation rate) is the return the market expects from that type of property, shown as a percentage.

A quick example:

| | |
|---|---|
| Net rent per year | $70,000 |
| Cap rate | 6.5% |
| Indicative value | $70,000 ÷ 0.065 = **about $1,076,923** |

Now watch what happens when the cap rate moves:

| Cap rate | Indicative value |
|---|---|
| 5.5% | $1,272,727 |
| 6.0% | $1,166,667 |
| 6.5% | $1,076,923 |
| 7.0% | $1,000,000 |
| 7.5% | $933,333 |

Same building. Same rent. A one-point change in the cap rate moves the value by more than $150,000.

And at a 6.5% cap rate, **every extra $1,000 of net rent adds about $15,385 of value**. That's why rent matters so much.

*These are simple examples to show the maths, not market cap rates or valuations.*

---

## Why net income, not just rent, is the number that counts

Two properties can both "earn $70,000 a year" and still be worth different amounts. It comes down to who pays the costs.

- **Net lease:** the tenant pays rent plus outgoings, such as council rates, water, building insurance, strata levies and land tax. The owner keeps most of the rent.
- **Gross lease:** the tenant pays one figure, and the owner pays the outgoings out of it.

Say a gross lease brings in $120,000 a year and the owner pays $15,000 in outgoings. The net income is $105,000. At a 7% cap rate, that's an indicative value of $1,500,000, not the $1,714,286 you'd get if you forgot the outgoings.

**The lesson:** always work from net income. A listing headline about rent doesn't tell you what the owner actually keeps.

> **Buying a property with a tenant in it?** Our [commercial buyers agent team](/buyers-agency) acts only for the buyer. We'll check the lease, the real net income and whether the price stacks up.

---

## What makes rental income worth more (or less)

Not all rent is equal. Two properties with the same net income can have very different cap rates because of the quality of that income. Valuers and buyers typically look at:

**1. How long the lease has left**
A tenant locked in for seven more years is worth more than one whose lease ends in six months. Less time left means more risk of an empty building.

**2. Who the tenant is**
A national business or government tenant is usually seen as lower risk than a new start-up. Lower risk generally means a lower cap rate and a higher value.

**3. How the rent grows**
Fixed annual increases or CPI reviews give the owner predictable growth. A lease with no reviews for years is less attractive.

**4. Whether the rent is at market**
Rent well above market may not survive the next review or a new tenant. Rent below market might be an opportunity, or a warning sign. Valuers often adjust for this.

**5. Incentives**
This one catches people out, so it gets its own section.

---

## Face rent vs effective rent: the incentive effect

When landlords offer rent-free months or a fitout contribution, the rent written in the lease (the face rent) can be higher than what the tenant really pays over the term (the effective rent).

Here's an example:

| | |
|---|---|
| Area | 200 m² |
| Face rent | $350/m², or $70,000 a year |
| Term | 5 years, 3% annual reviews |
| Rent-free | 6 months |
| Fitout contribution | $20,000 |
| Total face rent over 5 years | $371,640 |
| Incentives | $55,000, about 15% of the rent |
| **Effective rent** | **about $63,328 a year, or $317/m²** |

Valuers and experienced buyers often look past the face rent to the effective rent. So if you're buying, check what incentives were given. If you're leasing, understand that landlords sometimes prefer a higher face rent with bigger incentives because of how it reads on paper. That knowledge is useful when you negotiate.

---

## Why this matters if you're buying your own premises

Plenty of Newcastle business owners buy their own building, often through an SMSF or a family trust, and then lease it to their own business.

In that case the rent you pay yourself still matters:

- **It drives the value.** If you sell later, the buyer will look at the lease and the rent, just like any other investment.
- **It needs to be right.** If your SMSF owns the property and leases it to your business, the lease generally needs to be on commercial, arm's-length terms. Your accountant and financial planner should set this up with you.
- **It sets up your exit.** A well-documented lease at market rent with a solid term can make the property more attractive to the next buyer.

*This is general information only. Talk to your accountant and financial planner about your structure.*

---

## Why this matters if you're a tenant

Even if you're never going to buy a building, this is worth knowing.

Your lease is part of your landlord's asset. The rent you agree to, the length of your term and the incentives in your deal can all affect what the building is worth to them.

That's not a reason to pay more. It's a reason to understand what matters to the other side, so you can negotiate a fair deal that works for both of you.

## Frequently asked questions

### How is commercial property valued in Australia?
Commercial property is commonly valued using its income, by dividing the net income by a cap rate that reflects the market and the risk. Valuers also compare it with recent sales of similar properties. The lease term, tenant, rent reviews and incentives all affect the result.

### What is a cap rate?
A cap rate is the property's annual net income divided by its value, shown as a percentage. A property earning $70,000 a year in net income valued at $1,076,923 has a 6.5% cap rate. Lower cap rates usually mean lower perceived risk and higher values.

### What is net operating income?
Net operating income is the rent an owner receives in a year, less the property costs the owner pays and can't recover from the tenant. It doesn't include loan repayments, tax or depreciation.

### Does a longer lease make a commercial property worth more?
Generally, yes. A long lease to a strong tenant gives the owner more certainty of income, which buyers and valuers usually value more highly than a short or expiring lease.

### What's the difference between face rent and effective rent?
Face rent is the rent written in the lease. Effective rent is what the tenant actually pays on average after incentives like rent-free months and fitout contributions. Effective rent is often lower and is a better guide to the real deal.

### Does a gross or net lease affect property value?
The lease type changes who pays the outgoings. Under a gross lease the owner pays them out of the rent, so the net income is lower than the headline rent. Value should always be worked out from net income.

### Can I calculate the value of a commercial property online?
You can test scenarios using our free Commercial Rent Calculator and Cap Rate Calculator. They show how rent and cap rates affect value, but they're not valuations. For a value you can rely on, use a registered valuer.
